evidence_quotes.quote: Sixteen villages were selected out of which only two villages in Neturia Block have piped water supply. The rest of the villages must rely on hand pumps, dug wells or surface water sources to meet their water demand.

For instance, the local community prioritizes the repair and maintenance of existing water sources, while local government and Block administration emphasize on construction of new water harvesting structures.

The GPs follow a crisis management approach, and a significant lack of proper rules and regulations is realized that would direct and guide the GPs on how to spend the fund they receive under different schemes.
Though all the GP heads of six Blocks were approached, only 33 GP heads (out of a total of 47 GP heads) participated in the interview process.

We are not allowed to collect water from the handpumps located in the area where the upper castes people live. We have only one handpump for 64 households in our area. During the dry season, the hand pump stops to work and we have to rely on rivers and streams.
This is one of the major obstacles towards ensuring water security in the study area as the villages that achieved full coverage slip into partially covered or no coverage

criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural household and community drinking/domestic water supply access (hand pumps, piped water supply, dug wells, and domestic ponds) alongside agricultural water security across 16 villages in Purulia district, West Bengal, India.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes) because it examines local multi-level water governance, institutional coordination across communities, Gram Panchayats, and Block administration, community participation in O&M, and political patronage/corruption in rural water supply. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (narrow=no) because its focus is generic rural water project delivery, infrastructure vs. O&M action prioritization, community-management participation gaps, and broad physical/financial/technical implementation barriers rather than analysing a specific rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, utility regulatory structure, or formal enforcement/accommodation rules) directly governing household service access. Incidental descriptive mentions of rigid borehole depth budgets, informal village tap turn-taking in one village, patronage in siting/beneficiary lists, and lack of fiscal spending rules illustrate general scheme delivery challenges rather than a studied rule-type access mechanism.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical qualitative and questionnaire data from focus group discussions and open-ended surveys with 282 villagers (154 farmers and 128 women) across 16 villages, semi-structured interviews with 33 Gram Panchayat heads, and consensus questionnaires/discussions with Block officials across 6 Blocks.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports qualitative evidence on rural household water availability, hand pump functionality and dry-season breakdowns, piped supply reliability, slippage from full to partial/no coverage, and caste- or power-based exclusion from community hand pumps, alongside stakeholder percentages for prioritized actions and perceived implementation barriers.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and units of analysis (community women and farmers, Gram Panchayat heads, and Block officials), qualitative/questionnaire narrative study design, broad local governance/project-delivery exposure, and qualitative water access/functionality outcomes are clearly identifiable, though it lacks an eligible rule-type exposure under narrow Criterion 2.

study_design: Qualitative multi-level narrative study using focus group discussions, open-ended questionnaires, and semi-structured interviews
population_and_sample: 282 village respondents (154 farmers and 128 women) across 16 villages, 33 Gram Panchayat heads (of 47 approached), and Block administrative officials (Block Development Officers, Block Agriculture Officers, and Assistant Engineers) across 6 Blocks in Purulia district, West Bengal, India
exposure: Multi-actor local rural water supply governance, scheme implementation/project delivery priorities (new water harvesting construction vs. repair and maintenance), community O&M participation, and implementation barriers across village, Gram Panchayat, and Block administrative levels
outcome: Stakeholder-prioritized actions and perceived barriers to rural water security, alongside qualitative accounts of domestic water availability, hand pump functionality, piped water reliability, coverage slippage, and unequal/caste-excluded access to community water sources
rationale: This qualitative multi-actor empirical study examines rural household and agricultural water security across 16 villages and 6 Blocks in Purulia district, West Bengal, India. While it satisfies Criteria 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 and would be included under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (as an empirical study of local rural water governance, community management, and institutional coordination), it fails the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 and is therefore excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure). Rather than evaluating a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, tariffs, regulatory structure, or formal enforcement/discretion rules), the paper elicits stakeholder rankings of infrastructure/O&M project-delivery priorities and general financial, hydrogeological, technical, and community-participation barriers.
